On her first day at the Jaffle Shop, Sara, a new analyst, opens the warehouse and finds a table
. Is it in cents or in dollars? Does it include failed payments? Which statuses exist, and what does
mean? She sends five messages to the data team, waits two days, and finally guesses. Her first dashboard is wrong.

Documentation is the answer to every one of those messages, written once, next to the code, and published where people look. In dbt, documentation is not a separate Word file that nobody updates: it lives in the same YAML files as your tests, it is version-controlled with Git, it is reviewed in pull requests, and dbt turns it into a website with a lineage graph. On the dbt platform, the same information feeds dbt Catalog for the whole company. On the exam you will meet the commands, the files they produce, the
and the platform view. This chapter gives you all of them, tested on your own project.

Think of a public library. The books are your tables. Without a catalogue card for each book (title, author, subject, shelf), the library is just a room full of paper: you must open every book to know what is inside. dbt documentation is the catalogue card of each table and column, plus a map of the shelves (the lineage graph). And just as a library catalogue is updated every time a new book arrives, dbt rebuilds the documentation from the project every time you run

# Jaffle Shop analytics (practice project)
